content: The Academy of the Criminal Executive Service of Ukraine has trained 1,300 specialists, including psychologists working in juvenile correctional and detention centers, as well as probation officers from across the country. Concerns about testing children under the age of 14, the age of consent in Ukraine, were addressed through consultations with health managers and providers. However, implementing legislative changes to address age-related restrictions remains challenging due to political instability. The SMARTgirl program in Cambodia, developed by FHI 360, aims to prevent and mitigate the impact of HIV while improving the sexual and reproductive health of approximately 35,000 entertainment workers, many of whom are sex workers. Among some groups, HIV prevalence is as high as 14%. The program provides HIV prevention information, commodities, and referrals through trained peer educators. In some areas, mobile STI screening, HIV testing, and family planning services are also available. SMARTgirl also supports harm reduction strategies, including counseling, methadone maintenance treatment, and needle exchange programs for workers who inject drugs. Since 2009, the program has worked to reduce stigma and discrimination by giving entertainment workers a voice at national and local levels. Nearly half of all entertainment workers in Cambodia are reached through workplace outreach, and the program has a health and social network with approximately 10,000 members. In the year leading up to March 2012, 15,680 sex workers received services, covering 92% of the targeted group. The SHARPER project in Accra, Ghana, recruits young female sex workers who are leaders within their peer groups to serve as peer educators. These educators undergo a one-week training program, followed by weekly supervision and monthly reviews. They are paired with older community women, known as peer protectors, who provide guidance and support. Peer educators receive a stipend to cover transportation and communication costs and focus on priority issues such as safer sex negotiation, family planning, and referrals for HIV testing and counseling. They also address violence prevention and support young sex workers in accessing critical services. Despite challenges related to the mobility of young sex workers, the program offers peer-accompanied referrals and collaborates with other organizations to provide support in cases of human rights abuses, sexual violence, and childcare. The Sex Workers Outreach Programme (SWOP) in Nairobi, Kenya, affiliated with the University of Manitoba and the University of Nairobi, promotes the health, safety, and rights of sex workers. The program serves an estimated 30,000 sex workers and has expanded from three to nine service sites since 2008. SWOP provides peer-led, hotspot-based outreach services, offering HIV and STI prevention and care. Seven sites cater to sex workers, while two facilities serve HIV-infected family members, friends, and clients of sex workers. The program provides comprehensive HIV prevention and treatment services, including cervical cancer screening. In 2013, SWOP made 103,000 contacts with sex workers and conducted 31,000 HIV tests. The program has been instrumental in establishing clinical guidelines for syndromic STI treatment, which is now part of Kenya's national health policy. The AIDS Myanmar Association (AMA) is a network of over 2,000 sex workers, including female, male, and transgender individuals. The program focuses on capacity building and community mobilization to advocate for the health and rights of sex workers. AMA provides STI and HIV prevention tools, links to sex worker-friendly health facilities, and follow-up care for those living with HIV. Outreach workers are trained to be sensitive to the needs of young people and avoid asking for identifying information. AMA also supports sex workers in prison, ensuring nutritional support for young individuals abandoned by their families. The River of Life (ROLi) program in the Philippines serves 6,000 young males aged 13–17, most of whom sell sex and use drugs. The program uses peer-to-peer outreach, risk self-assessment tools, and workshops to help participants reduce risky behaviors. Outreach is conducted in communities, online, and through social media. Participants can join moderated Facebook groups for discussions about behavior change. The program has been adapted to serve other key populations, including female sex workers and young people who inject drugs. In South Africa, the Re-Action. program, in collaboration with the Department of Health, provides mobile outreach services to female sex workers in rural districts of Mpumalanga Province. The program offers free health risk screening, HIV testing, and treatment, as well as life skills mentoring to reduce vulnerability to violence, exploitation, and substance abuse. A mobile clinic visits clients at convenient times and locations, and outreach workers provide follow-up support for those who default on treatment. St. James Infirmary in San Francisco, USA, is a peer-led clinic offering free, confidential, and non-judgmental medical and social services to sex workers. Services include primary care, HIV and STI testing, hormone therapy, acupuncture, and support groups. The clinic was established to address the stigma and criminalization faced by sex workers, creating a harm-reduction-based environment where individuals feel safe and supported. The Sisters with a Voice program in Zimbabwe, run by the Centre for Sexual Health and HIV/AIDS Research (CeSHHAR), provides integrated services for sex workers, including HTC, STI treatment, contraceptives, and legal advice. The program has expanded to a national network of 36 sites and has served over 14,000 women. It has significantly increased HIV testing and ART uptake among sex workers. The Silueta X Association in Ecuador promotes health among young transgender individuals and educates them on the risks of feminizing hormone regimens. The program uses peer communication and social media to reach its target audience and has trained activists and community members to provide accurate information. The Health Outreach to Teens (HOTT) program in New York City serves LGBTQ adolescents, homeless youth, and those living with HIV. It provides acute and primary care, mental health services, and health education in a trans-affirming environment. The program also offers a weekly transgender women's support group and engages clients through a Youth Advisory Board. The Center of Excellence for Transgender Health in the USA aims to improve access to comprehensive and affirming healthcare for transgender communities. It develops guidelines on primary care, hormone therapy, and mental health and supports community-based organizations in implementing evidence-based HIV prevention interventions. Aksion Plus, founded in 1992, was the first youth NGO in Albania to address HIV through education and awareness. The program now supports health and human rights interventions for young people who inject drugs, sex workers, and LGBTQ individuals. It provides direct services, harm reduction training, and peer education to empower key populations.
